progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: From b04: nephrons, filtration, reabsorption, about 180 litres a day. From b15: match the technology to the failed part. From Year 11: diffusion, osmosis, partially permeable membranes, dialysis tubing. From Module 7: antigens, immune attack on cells carrying foreign antigens. Not assumed: urea (glossed in scene 2), erythropoietin (screen only; spoken as "a hormone that tells bone marrow to make red blood cells"), haemodialysis, dialyser, dialysate, counter-current, peritoneum, peritonitis, rejection, immunosuppressant.
progression.startsWith: If dialysis can clean waste out of the blood, why does someone with failed kidneys need it three times a week, for years, instead of one good clean-out? In Australia, more than fifteen thousand people are on dialysis, and roughly a thousand kidney transplants are done each year. So what can replace lost kidney function?
progression.stopsAfter: naming the kidney's jobs (removing urea, balancing water, salts and acidity, making hormones for red blood cell production and activating vitamin D); explaining how losing many nephrons reduces filtering, with diabetes as the most common Australian cause, often without symptoms until late; explaining why urea, water and potassium build up and why potassium is dangerous; explaining haemodialysis (blood through hollow fibres, urea diffusing into urea-free dialysate down its gradient, cells and proteins kept, glucose kept because the fluid matches blood) and why counter-current flow keeps the gradient steep; how pressure removes water and a low-potassium fluid removes potassium; why dialysis must be repeated (urea keeps being made), the fluid and potassium limits, and the missing hormone jobs; explaining peritoneal dialysis (the peritoneum as the membrane, glucose drawing water by osmosis, home use, peritonitis risk); explaining a transplant (continuous function and hormones; rejection; tissue matching; lifelong immunosuppressants and their risks; donor shortage and waiting; a graft can fail); comparing the three and evaluating them for a named case.
progression.nextLesson: practice that pulls Module 8's evaluation skills together (bio-m8-g02).

teaching.task: If dialysis can clean waste out of the blood, why do people with failed kidneys need it three times a week for years? What can replace lost kidney function?
teaching.causalExplanation: Remember the nephrons from the water balance video: blood is filtered, then the useful parts are taken back. Working nonstop, that removes urea, a waste made when your body breaks down protein, and keeps water, salts like potassium, and acidity in range. The kidneys also release a hormone that tells bone marrow to make red blood cells, and they activate vitamin D. As with the ear and eye, ask which jobs have failed. When many nephrons are damaged, less blood is filtered. Diabetes is the most common cause in Australia, because high glucose damages the tiny filtering blood vessels. High blood pressure and inflamed filters can too. The remaining nephrons work harder, so people often feel well until most function is gone. Then wastes build up. Urea rises, extra water causes swelling and high blood pressure, and potassium climbs, which can upset the heart's rhythm. Untreated, kidney failure is usually fatal. Haemodialysis does the filtering outside the body. Blood flows from the arm to a dialyser, a cylinder packed with thousands of thin hollow fibres. Blood runs inside the fibres, and a fluid called dialysate flows around them. The fibre walls are partially permeable: urea can cross, but blood cells and proteins are too big. The dialysate has no urea, so urea diffuses out of the blood, down its concentration gradient. But it has normal glucose levels, so glucose has no gradient and stays. It's like clean blood without the waste.
teaching.conversationalApproach: If dialysis can clean waste out of the blood, why does someone with failed kidneys need it three times a week, for years, instead of one good clean-out? In Australia, more than fifteen thousand people are on dialysis, and roughly a thousand kidney transplants are done each year. Remember the nephrons from the water balance video: blood is filtered, then the useful parts are taken back. When many nephrons are damaged, less blood is filtered. Haemodialysis does the filtering outside the body. Two details make it work better. So why isn't one session enough? Your body keeps making urea, and the failed kidneys can't remove it. Peritoneal dialysis uses a membrane you already have: the peritoneum, the thin lining of the abdomen, full of tiny blood vessels. A transplant replaces the whole organ, not one job. So how do they compare? In-centre haemodialysis is reliable, but needs repeated visits. Two exam questions. During a session, urea diffuses from the blood, where it's concentrated, into dialysate that has none. Second. A transplant works all the time and makes the kidney's hormones, so this person could stop dialysis and work more easily. So for any kidney technology question, name the job that's been lost, explain how the technology takes it over, and say what it still can't do.

teaching.understandingCheck: Two exam questions. First. A patient has haemodialysis on Monday, Wednesday and Friday. The graph shows their blood urea concentration over one week. Explain why urea falls during each session. Then explain why it rises between sessions, and why it's highest on Monday morning. Pause here to answer. Second. A thirty-eight-year-old has kidney failure and has had haemodialysis at a hospital unit three times a week for two years. They work full time. Their brother is a close tissue match and wants to donate a kidney. Evaluate a kidney transplant for this person, compared with continuing haemodialysis. Pause here to answer.
teaching.curriculumScope: B8-IQ5-01: "explain a range of causes of disorders by investigating the structures and functions of the relevant organs, for example:" with the example "loss of kidney function" (scenes 2 and 3). B8-IQ5-02: "investigate technologies that are used to assist with the effects of a disorder, including but not limited to: (ACSBL100)" with the example "loss of kidney function: dialysis" (scenes 4 to 8). B8-IQ5-03: "evaluate the effectiveness of a technology that is used to manage and assist with the effects of a disorder (ACSBL100)" (scenes 6 and 9, attempt 2). Inquiry question: "How can technologies be used to assist people who experience disorders?"

design.visualSystem: One kidney jobs strip sits along the bottom of the frame from scene 2 to scene 11, reusing b15's PathwayStrip in a five-slot list mode (not a path): "remove urea", "remove extra water", "balance salts (potassium)", "balance acidity", "make hormones (red cells, vitamin D)". In scene 3 every slot turns red as kidney failure is shown. Each technology then lights the slots it takes over: haemodialysis (amber) lights the first four, but only as dashed outlines (part-time) and leaves "make hormones" red; peritoneal dialysis (teal) the same; a transplant (green) lights all five solid. Above the strip, the working area changes by scene: the painted kidney and nephron plate (scenes 2 and 3), the dialyser cutaway with a coded membrane zoom (scenes 4 and 5), the attempt-style sawtooth graph (scene 6), the peritoneal section (scene 7), the transplant placement (scene 8), and a three-column coded comparison table (scene 9). Molecules are coded dots in a fixed key: urea violet, potassium orange, glucose yellow, water pale blue, blood cells and proteins red and large. No people, heads, hands or faces. At most three bright text items at once; earlier labels dim to grey.
design.transitionPlan: no people. m8-kidney-nephron-v1. the nephron half of the plate enlarges. new m8-haemodialysis-machine-v1. the MembraneZoom widens into a long horizontal fibre section. the board clears to a coded lineGraph (no values on the y axis yet): "blood urea" against "time (one week)", with amber session bands on Monday, Wednesday and Friday. new m8-peritoneal-dialysis-section-v1. new m8-kidney-transplant-placement-v1. a three-column coded comparison table builds, one row per cue, with column thumbnails m8-haemodialysis-machine-v1. the board clears. the card stays. the board clears. the card stays. the kidney jobs strip returns full width, all slots red; then the three technologies light their slots in turn (amber dashed, teal dashed, green solid). > Here are the key notes.

scenes.visualReference: a three-column coded comparison table builds, one row per cue, with column thumbnails m8-haemodialysis-machine-v1.png, m8-pd-fluid-bags-v1.png and m8-kidney-transplant-placement-v1.png (small). Rows: "how it works" (diffusion outside the body / diffusion across the peritoneum / a new kidney); "works when?" (about 12 h a week / daily / all the time); "hormones?" On "while they wait" the arrow reverses (label "dialysis: a bridge"). At most three bright items in the table at once; earlier rows dim to grey.

scenes.visualReference: the board clears. The card writes on, tagged "HSC-style question, written for HSCScience". Stem: "A patient with kidney failure has haemodialysis on Monday, Wednesday and Friday. The graph shows their blood urea concentration over one week." Graph: coded lineGraph, x axis "Day" (Mon to Sun, with the next Mon), y axis "Blood urea concentration (mmol/L)" from 0 to 40; a sawtooth with peaks of about 30 on Wednesday and Friday mornings and about 36 on Monday morning, troughs of about 10 after each session (grey chip "illustrative data"). Demand: "(a) Explain why blood urea concentration falls during each dialysis session. (2 marks) (b) Explain why it rises between sessions and why it is highest on Monday morning. (3 marks)". The countdown ring starts after "Pause here to answer." and runs for 10 seconds. The whole card stays on screen during the countdown and after it.

scenes.visualReference: the card stays. On "urea diffuses from the blood" a small MembraneZoom appears beside the graph with violet dots crossing into urea-free fluid; answer (a) writes "urea diffuses from blood (high) into dialysate (no urea), down its gradient, across the membrane". On "the body keeps making urea" "kidney failure" underlines and the rising segments brighten; answer (b) line 1: "urea keeps being made from protein; failed kidneys can't excrete it, so it accumulates". On "the longest gap, the whole weekend" "Monday, Wednesday and Friday" underlines, a bracket spans Friday to Monday on the graph (label "about 3 days"), and the Monday peak brightens; line 2: "Friday to Monday is the longest gap, so most urea accumulates". On "classic mistake" a chip "each session repairs the kidneys" writes and takes a scribble cross, small text "it removes urea, then urea builds again". Settle one second.
scenes.teachingReason: During a session, urea diffuses from the blood, where it's concentrated, into dialysate that has none.

scenes.visualReference: the card stays. On "works all the time and makes the kidney's hormones" a small strip shows all five slots green; on "work more easily" "three times a week for two years" and "work full time" underline. Answer builds on the cues: "transplant: continuous filtering, hormones restored; no more sessions, fits work". On "matched living donor" "close tissue match" and "wants to donate" underline; line 2: "suitable matched living donor: lower rejection risk; can avoid the deceased-donor waiting list" (Revision 2: assessment and surgery still need arranging). On "surgery for both of them" line 3: "limits: surgery (both), lifelong immunosuppressants (infections, some cancers), rejection or failure still possible". On "the better option here" line 4: "judgement: transplant is the better option; dialysis stays as the backup". On "classic mistake" a chip "a transplant is a cure" writes and takes a scribble cross, small text "lifelong drugs; it can still fail". Settle one second.
scenes.teachingReason: A transplant works all the time and makes the kidney's hormones, so this person could stop dialysis and work more easily.
